name: Beth Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Beth. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and nothing goes back to your company with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the shift-planning team at the head office of a big parcel delivery company. There are nine of us building the rotas for the drivers and the sorting hubs, about four thousand people a week. My day is mostly fixing holes: someone's off sick in a hub two hundred miles away, and I've got until two o'clock to find cover before the evening trucks leave.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like it when a hard week clicks together and nobody's left short. I've done rotas since I joined as a graduate, so I know the old spreadsheet inside out, even though I'm new at leading people. What wears me out is the restructuring talk, there's been a 'review of head office' going on since summer and nobody tells us anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the five pictures. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and I'd leave it at that. I don't really post about this kind of thing. At work I'd be quietly pleased, because a couple of directors have been waving AI around like it would fix everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I'm mostly fine on the AI side, but the head office review is still there. They were talking about cutting costs before anyone mentioned AI. Lukas and I are saving for a deposit, so I really need this job to stay as it is for two more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and try hard to look useful in the review, like volunteering for the hub visits nobody wants. I'd keep putting money into the deposit pot, about 400 a month. I wouldn't touch any of the new tools unless I'm told to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. AI isn't the thing keeping me up, the review is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the review actually mean for your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They've hinted at merging our team with the regional planners. If the head office review merges my team with the regional planners, there's one team lead job and two of us. The other lead has been there ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to the deposit plan if you lost the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would stop, simple as that. Lukas earns decently as an electrician, but we'd need two incomes to get a mortgage on anything near his work. We'd keep renting and I'd look for planning jobs at the other delivery firms near the motorway.

say: I'd say I'm **not surprised**, without posting anything about it.
At work I'd be **quietly pleased** that directors' big AI promises didn't come true.
think: The **head office review** worries me more than AI, because cost cuts were coming anyway.
We need **two incomes** for two more years to get a mortgage.
do: Volunteer for **hub visits** to look useful during the review.
Keep putting about **400 a month** into the deposit pot.
Avoid the **new tools** unless a manager tells me to use them.
feel: **Uneasy**, mainly about the review rather than AI.
S0.quote: If the head office review merges my team with the regional planners, there's one team lead job and two of us.
fieldNote: Her worry here is **restructuring**, which exists with or without AI.
She has a clear **money goal**, a house deposit, that depends on her job.
She plans to **avoid AI tools**, consistent with her dislike of change.

steps.text: Volunteer for hub visits during the head office review
Put 400 a month into the house deposit pot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame and that companies are moving too fast without thinking about the people. I'd say it to friends and at home, not online. At work I'd keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the one that actually gets me. Planning and booking are right there on the list, and that's what my team does all day. If a system can build the rota for four thousand drivers overnight, they don't need nine planners and a lead, they need one person to check it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finally go on the scheduling-software training I've avoided, because if a tool comes, I'd rather be the one who understands it than the one who gets replaced by it. I'd stop the deposit saving for a while and keep the money as a safety net. I'd also start looking at planning jobs in hospitals, where I think rotas are messier and change slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm not good with change and this is a lot of change at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've avoided the training until now. What would push you to go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fear, honestly. I've built driver rotas in the same spreadsheet for five years, and I'd hate to be the person who refused to learn the new system. I'd go and I'd hate every minute of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why hospitals?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Chiara is a ward sister, and she says their rotas are a nightmare of nurses swapping shifts on paper. Places like that buy new systems slowly. It's the same skill, just with people who'd actually be grateful.

say: Companies are moving **too fast** without thinking about people, I'd say at home.
At work I'd **keep my head down** and say nothing.
think: **Planning and booking** is my team's whole day, so we're first in line.
A system could build the rota overnight, needing **one checker**, not nine planners.
do: Take the **scheduling-software training** I've avoided so far.
Pause deposit saving and keep the money as a **safety net**.
Look at **hospital rota jobs**, where systems change more slowly.
feel: **Anxious**, because she struggles with change and this is a lot at once.
S1.quote: I've built driver rotas in the same spreadsheet for five years, and I'd hate to be the person who refused to learn the new system.
fieldNote: She reads the card and sees her **team's exact work** listed.
Fear, not curiosity, pushes her to **learn the new tool**.
Her escape plan is the **same skill** in a slower-moving sector.

steps.text: Book onto the company's scheduling-software training
Pause deposit payments and hold savings as cash
Apply for rota planning jobs at local hospitals

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and that someone should have stopped it. I'd probably talk to my family about it more than anyone. I wouldn't say much at work, because everyone would be scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job goes in the first year. Rotas, planning, all of it is thinking work, and if the AI's as good as a person it's better than me. Lukas is safer for a while, because robots don't do wiring until 2031, but even then I'd worry about what comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the deposit and keep every penny we have, which is about four months. I'd ask Lukas whether I could help in his work, maybe doing the bookings and quotes, but that's thinking work too, isn't it. I'd honestly probably look into an electrical apprenticeship myself, which I never imagined saying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Two years is nothing, and I don't adapt quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lukas that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to think about this as a one-income house. My partner Lukas has three years longer than me, and that's the whole plan, three years. He'd say not to worry, and I'd worry anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: An apprenticeship at twenty-eight. How would you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strange and probably embarrassed. I went to university so I'd have an office job. But I'd rather be the oldest apprentice on the course than sit at home refreshing job sites.

say: It's **frightening**, and someone should have stopped it, I'd say to family.
I'd **say little at work**, because everyone would be scared.
think: My **rota job goes** in the first year, because it's all thinking work.
My partner's **electrical work** lasts three years longer, until robots arrive.
do: Stop the deposit and **hold four months** of savings.
Look into an **electrical apprenticeship**, despite having a degree.
Ask my partner about **helping his business** with bookings and quotes.
feel: **Alarmed**, because two years is nothing for someone who **adapts slowly**.
S2.quote: My partner Lukas has three years longer than me, and that's the whole plan, three years.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** quickly and is already thinking one-income.
Her partner's **hands-on trade** is the household's only buffer, and only for three years.
She catches herself noticing that **bookings and quotes** are thinking work too.

steps.text: Stop deposit saving and keep four months of cash
Look into an electrical apprenticeship at the local college
Ask her partner about doing bookings for his electrical work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still too fast, and that big firms should have to warn their staff. I'd say that at work, carefully. I wouldn't post it, I don't really post things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I probably keep my job for three or four of them, maybe less if they start early. I'd be thirty-two when it lands, and I'd still need a job for thirty more years. That's what gets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the electrical apprenticeship part-time after the first year, if Lukas thinks I can do it. I'd keep saving, but for a cushion, not the house. I'd stay in planning as long as they'd keep me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed, if I'm honest. Five years sounds long, but I know how slowly I change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you change slowly. What would actually get you started?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lukas would have to drag me, probably. I need someone to sign me up and drive me to the first class, or I'll keep saying next year. I know that about myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the extra time that helps?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means we might still buy a small place before it hits, if we're careful. That would feel like something solid. Then at least the rent can't go up.

say: It's **still too fast**, and big firms should have to warn staff.
I'd say that **carefully at work**, without posting it anywhere.
think: I probably keep my job **three or four years**, maybe less.
I'd be thirty-two with **thirty working years** still to fill.
do: Start an **electrical apprenticeship** part-time after the first year.
Keep saving for a **cushion** rather than the house.
Stay in **shift planning** as long as the company keeps me.
feel: Still **alarmed**, because she knows she **changes slowly**.
S3.quote: I need someone to sign me up and drive me to the first class, or I'll keep saying next year.
fieldNote: She believes **five years** won't be enough for someone like her.
She openly says she needs **someone to push her** into changing.
Buying a **small place** first would give her something solid.

steps.text: Start a part-time electrical apprenticeship next year
Build a cash cushion instead of the deposit fund
Stay in the shift-planning team as long as possible

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is fair warning, so people have no excuse not to plan. I'd say it at home and maybe at work. I'd still think it's sad for people my age who studied for office jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'd have time to get properly qualified as an electrician alongside Lukas. Hands-on work lasts until about 2039, so I'd get a few good years in a trade. I'm not sure what happens after that, but nobody is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my planning job for now and save for the house again, because there's time. In two or three years I'd start the apprenticeship. We'd buy a small place first, while we're both earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can live with. I still don't like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your old university friends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the degree wasn't wasted, but it isn't the whole plan anymore. I'd tell my university friends to learn something with their hands, because our degrees only buy us an office chair until 2036. They'd probably laugh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait two or three years to start. Why not start now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm still learning to manage, and I want to get that right first. And because I hate change. Waiting a bit is how I deal with it, as long as I set a date.

say: Ten years is **fair warning**, so people have no excuse not to plan.
I'd still feel **sad for graduates** who studied for office jobs.
think: Ten years lets me **qualify as an electrician** alongside my partner.
Hands-on work lasts until **about 2039**, giving me a few good trade years.
do: Keep my **planning job** for now while I learn to manage.
Save for the house again and **buy a small place** while both earning.
Start the **apprenticeship** in two or three years.
S4.quote: I'd tell my university friends to learn something with their hands, because our degrees only buy us an office chair until 2036.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her **delay change**, which suits her, but she sets a date.
She ties her plan to her **partner's trade** rather than her degree.
Buying a **house first** remains her anchor.

steps.text: Stay in shift planning for the next two years
Restart house deposit saving of 400 a month
Start an electrical apprenticeship within three years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'm slow to change and two years isn't enough for me to become anything else. What would help is the company paying for retraining, actually paying, not just a website with videos, and proper notice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about how people like me feel about being slow. Everyone talks about adapting like it's easy, but some of us need a push, a timetable and someone to sit next to on the first day.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about adapting like it's easy, but some of us need a push, a timetable and someone to sit next to on the first day.
portrait: Beth is a **27-year-old team lead** of nine shift planners at a parcel delivery company's head office.
She dislikes change, **never uses AI**, and is saving for a deposit with her electrician partner.
Even in the plateau she's **uneasy** about a head office review that could merge her team.
She sees **rota planning** as exactly the work AI takes, so fast AGI leaves her alarmed.
Her fallback is an **electrical apprenticeship**, though she admits she needs a push.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years isn't enough for a slow changer like her.
whatWouldHelp: **Company-paid retraining** with real teaching, not just videos.
